Issued at 235 AM CST Fri Nov 20 2026

While cloud cover has greatly increased compared to yesterday, 
temperatures have still cooled quite a bit overnight. Temperatures 
across the region are in the mid 30s to lower 40s with a couple more 
degrees of cooling expected over the next couple of hours. However, 
a strong southerly LLJ ahead of an approaching upper-level trough 
will cause WAA into MN/WI throughout today. Did slightly decrease 
today's highs given the expected mostly cloudy skies. A few showers 
and drizzle are even possible across central MN this morning along 
the nose of the WAA. But, southern MN into west-central WI should 
still see low 60s by this afternoon. MSP's record high for today is 
63 and they are currently forecast to reach 64! To the northwest in 
western and central MN (where the showers are possible), highs will 
reach the mid to upper 50s. Meanwhile, surface winds will greatly 
increase into this afternoon due to the aforementioned LLJ. 
Strongest winds are expected to be south of the Minnesota River 
Valley, especially along I-90. Here, sustained values will reach 25-
30 MPH while gusts reach 35 to in excess of 45 MPH. Have coordinated 
with neighboring offices and issued a Wind Advisory for Martin 
county. This is where gusts in excess of 45 MPH are most likely this 
afternoon. Please secure outdoor objects and high profile vehicles 
should use caution when driving. Winds lessen as one travels north, 
but gusts of 20-30 MPH are still expected for central MN and WI. 
Winds will slow a bit as we go into Friday night.

A shower or two is possible across central MN this evening into 
tonight as a surface low deepens to our north. However, better rain 
chances start after sunrise Saturday as a cold front begins to sweep 
through from west to east. CAMs favor scattered to isolated showers 
developing over central/eastern MN Saturday morning, with activity 
gradually picking up as the cold front slides east into WI Saturday 
afternoon and evening. The issue is much of the guidance doesn't 
favor more widespread rain beginning until the front is well into 
WI. Thus, it still seems like our far eastern WI counties could see 
a few tenths of an inch of rain but heaviest amounts will likely be 
to the east of our CWA. Prior to the cold front passing through, 
southeastern MN and west-central WI will have highs in the mid 50s 
to lower 60s. But, these highs will occur in the early mornings of 
Saturday with temperatures continually falling throughout the day. 
Northwesterly winds will be breezy behind the front so it definitely 
will feel more "fall-like" Saturday. Rain should continue in west-
central WI Saturday night before moving east by Sunday morning. 
Temperatures will be much cooler Sunday with highs reaching the mid 
30s to lower 40s. A few cosmetic snowflakes be possible in our far 
north and east as a trailing shortwave slides into the Upper Great 
Lakes. But, any meaningful snow will be well to our north.

Temperatures look to bottom out early to mid-next week as highs are 
forecast to be generally in the lower to mid 30s. Meanwhile, 
overnight lows will be cold in the mid-teens to lower 20s through 
Wednesday night. Long-range guidance favors temperatures increasing 
slightly after mid-next week, though still remaining close to normal 
for this time of year. Alas, our run of well above normal 
temperatures seems to be done for foreseeable future. As for 
additional precipitation chances, they are currently pretty bleak 
next week. The Upper Midwest will be in post-trough northwest flow 
Monday into Tuesday with high pressure moving overhead. Then, upper-
level split flow develops over the central CONUS mid-week onward, 
leaving us between the two jetstreams. A lack of large-scale 
synoptic forcing is making it very difficult to develop certainty in 
PoPs within the long-range guidance. Odds are that our entire area 
won't be completely dry for the entire week, but more time needs to 
pass to resolve smaller scale features and increase forecast 
confidence in any PoPs.
